<> <> <> /* ─── STEP 0: First time or repeat after loss ─── */ <> <>

A tanned woman on the far side of the net is stretching — blonde ponytail, athletic build, tan lines visible across her shoulders. She catches you looking and walks over.
<>Hey. You play? I'm Liv. I've been stuck playing with these old men for months and they can barely return a serve. Want to team up?<>
<>Sure. I'm $name.<>
<>I don't care what your name is yet. I care if you can spike. Let's go.<>
<> <>

Liv spots you from the net and waves you over.
<>Ready for another round? Let's get it right this time.<>
<> You take your position on the sand. Liv serves. The game is on.

The ball comes your way — high arc, dropping fast.

<> <><><> <><> <><><> <><><> <><> <><> /* ─── STEP 1: Second match — BJ reward ─── */ <>

Liv is already at the net. She sees you and tosses the ball at your chest. You catch it.
<>Rematch. You and me versus those two again. But this time let's make it interesting — losers buy drinks at the bar tonight.<>
<>And if we win?<>
She smiles.
<>Winners get whatever they want.<>
First rally. Their server goes for an ace — hard topspin aimed at the back corner.

<> <> They tie it up and take the final rally on a lucky net cord. Liv kicks the sand. <>Bullshit. That was ours. Get back here next time and we're finishing this.<> <>
@@color:#e8c320;STR +1@@
@@color:white;Come back and try again.@@
<> <> <><><> <> They rally back. You lose in a tiebreak. Liv throws the ball at the net in frustration. <>We had them. Come back. I owe them a loss.<> <>
@@color:#e8c320;STR +1@@
@@color:white;Come back and try again.@@
<> <> <><> <><><> <> You lose the tiebreak. Liv shakes her head but she's not angry. <>So close. Get back here and we finish this.<> <>
@@color:#e8c320;STR +1@@
@@color:white;Come back and try again.@@
<> <> <><><> <> Their server aces you on the next point. Then the next. Game over. <>Damn. We'll get them. Come back.<> <>
@@color:#e8c320;STR +1@@
@@color:white;Come back and try again.@@
<> <> <><> <><> /* ─── STEP 2: Third match — sex reward ─── */ <>

Liv is leaning against the net post, arms crossed. She sees you and her eyes light up. Different energy this time — she's been waiting.
<>There you are. I was starting to think you were avoiding me after last time.<>
<>Avoiding you? You're the best thing on this beach.<>
<>Flattery works. But you still have to earn it on the court. One more game. If we win — my place. No excuses, no interruptions.<>
She holds the ball out to you. Eyebrow raised.
<>Deal?<>
<>Deal.<>
First point. Hard serve incoming.

<> <> Net cord. Their point. They take the set on a fluke and you lose by one. Liv stands there breathing hard, hands on her knees. <>One point. One fucking point. Get back here. We're not ending it like this.<> <>
@@color:#e8c320;STR +1@@
@@color:white;Come back and try again.@@
<> <> <><><> <> You swing wild. It goes long. Out. Their point. They win the tiebreak. <>That was supposed to be our game. Come back. We finish this.<> <>
@@color:#e8c320;STR +1@@
@@color:white;Come back and try again.@@
<> <> <><> <><><> <> He powers through your block. Their point. You lose in overtime. <>That block was close. Come back and close it for real.<> <>
@@color:#e8c320;STR +1@@
@@color:white;Come back and try again.@@
<> <> <><><> <> The dive isn't enough. Ball skids off your fingers and hits the sand on your side. Game over. <>Good effort. Wrong result. Come back.<> <>
@@color:#e8c320;STR +1@@
@@color:white;Come back and try again.@@
<> <> <><> <><> /* ─── STEP 3: Completed — just volleyball ─── */ <> Liv waves at you from the net. You play a game together — comfortable now, familiar. She bumps your hip with hers between rallies. You win easily.

<>We're unbeatable, $name. Come back anytime.<>

<> <> The path to the ship. White sand, afternoon sun. Adriana walks beside you carrying a small canvas bag — everything she owns.

Your father is standing by the landing pad. Hands in his pockets. He watches Adriana approach and something softens in his face.
<>Adriana.<>
<>Sir.<>
<>Don't call me that. You never had to call me that.<>
<>Thank you. For taking care of me. For all of it. You deserved better than what this place gave you.<>
<>So did you, sir.<>
<>No. I got exactly what I deserved. You didn't. Go see the rest of the galaxy, Adriana.<>
She nods. Picks up the bag. Walks toward the ship without looking back.
Your father turns to you.
<>You have the letter?<>
<>I have it.<>
<>The drives?<>
<>All three.<>
<> <>The codes?<>
<>Yeah.<>
<>Good. Give Jasper my regards. Tell him he was right about everything.<>
<> He looks at the ship. Then at you.
<>Be brave, $name. And make it home in one piece. Your $mom has waited long enough.<>
<>I will.<>
He pulls you in. A hug. Brief, tight. He lets go and steps back. Puts his hands back in his pockets.
<>Go on.<>

You walk up the ramp. Adriana is already inside, standing in the cabin, holding her bag against her chest. She looks at the seats, the console, the walls — all of it new. All of it not Paradiso.

You close the ramp. Slide into the pilot seat. Run the startup sequence — fuel check, thruster calibration, navigation alignment. The engines fire and the whole cabin shakes. Adriana grabs the armrest of the copilot chair.
<>It's loud.<>
<>It gets louder.<>
The ship lifts. Sand billows outward from the pad. Through the viewport you see one figure on the concrete — hands in pockets, watching. Getting smaller.

<>Is that normal? The shaking?<>
<>That's atmosphere. It stops once we break through.<>
The shaking stops. The blue sky goes dark. Stars appear — not gradually, all at once, like someone flipped a switch. Adriana leans forward in her seat and stares through the viewport. Her mouth is open. Her eyes are wide.
<>There are so many.<>
<>Yeah.<>
<>My mother told me about the stars. She said there were more than you could count. I thought she was exaggerating.<>
<>She wasn't.<>
Paradiso shrinks in the viewport. Green marble against dark water. Then just a dot. Then gone.
You set the hyperjump coordinates. The nav computer beeps. Adriana looks at the sealed envelope on the console — your $mom's name in your father's handwriting.
<>$name?<>
<>Yeah?<>
<>Where are we going?<>
<>Home. Or the closest thing to it.<>
She settles back in the copilot seat. Pulls her bag onto her lap. Looks out at the stars like someone seeing colour for the first time.
<>It's quiet now.<>
<>Yeah. That's space.<>
<>I like it.<>
The hyperdrive engages. The stars streak and bend. Paradiso disappears behind you.

The sunset is doing its thing — the sky cycling through colours that shouldn't exist together. Tangerine and violet and a deep bruised pink along the horizon. The silver rivers below have gone dark. The jungle is a wall of shadow.

<>Beautiful, isn't it.<>
It's not a question. He says it the way someone describes a habit they can't break.

<>It is.<>
<>That's the trick. The beauty is real — the light, the colours, the way the air smells at this hour. All real. And because it's real, it's hard to hold it against them. Hard to be angry at a sunset. Hard to hate the people who put you here when 'here' looks like a painting.<>
He drains his glass. Sets it down. The bartender reaches for the bottle but your father waves him off. First time you've seen him refuse a refill.

<>Some days I still notice. The bad days. The ones where I wake up and remember why I'm here instead of home. Those days the sunset looks like a bribe and the villa feels like a tomb and I sit on the terrace and think about all the things I'd do differently if the universe handed out second chances.<>
<>And the good days?<>
He looks at you. Something flickers in his expression — not guilt exactly. More like the memory of guilt, worn smooth by repetition.
<>The good days I don't think at all. I have breakfast. I read. I sit in the garden. And I let the island do what it was built to do — make me forget.<>

<>Dad.<>
<>Yeah?<>
<>Thanks for showing me around.<>
He nods. The smallest smile. Then he walks toward the cliff path and the villa, hands in his pockets, silhouetted against the last of the light. You watch him go. He looks smaller from behind. Or maybe it's just the sky.

You finish your drink. The bartender collects the glasses without a word. The music stops. Somewhere in the jungle, a bird you've never heard before sings three notes and goes quiet.

passages.name: p_station_task_gabbie
passages.source_raw:
<> <> The docking bay. Your ship sits on the pad, panels open along the underside. Gabbie is underneath on a rolling board, legs sticking out, a wrench clanging against something metallic. The floor around her is littered with sand — actual sand, from Paradiso, shaken loose from the engine housing.


<>How bad is it?<>
She rolls out. Grease on her forehead, on her arms, on the rag tucked into her belt. She sits up and wipes her hands on her thighs.
<>Sand in the primary intake, sand in the secondary filters, sand in places sand has no business being. Other than that, she's fine. I replaced the seals on the port thruster and recalibrated the nav alignment. Should hold for a few thousand light-years at least.<>
She tosses the wrench into the toolbox. Doesn't look at you.
<>So you're leaving today.<>
<>Yeah. I have to get the drives to Jasper. It can't wait.<>
<>I know it can't wait. Galaxy-saving stuff.<>
<>Gabbie.<>
<>I'm not mad. I'm just— when you promised you were going to come back I didn't expect you to immediatly lift off again.<>
She stands. Kicks a pile of sand with her boot.
<>This place gets empty when people leave, $name. Not just quiet. Empty. I'm not asking you to stay. I'm just saying — it's nice when the docking bay has a ship in it. That's all.<>
<>I'll come back, the ship is old, it might need upgrades soon.<>
<>Everyone says that.<>
<>I came back this time.<>
She looks at you. Considers it. Then she picks up the wrench and points it at you.
<>Don't land on any more beaches. I mean it.<>
<>Deal.<>
She rolls back under the ship. You hear the wrench start clanging again. Conversation over.
<> <> <> <>

passages.name: p_station_task_adriana
passages.source_raw:
<> <> You find them on the observation deck — if you can call a room with a scratched porthole and two bolted-down chairs an observation deck. Your $sis is leaning against the wall. Adriana is standing at the window, face close to the glass, staring at the stars.



<>She's been standing there for ten minutes.<>
<>Adriana?<>
<>On Paradiso you can see the stars at night, but not like this. We are actually here next to them. It's amazing.<>
<>There's a lot of them.<>
<>There's too many. It's overwhelming. How do you know which direction to go?<>
<>You don't, most of the time. You just pick one and hope for the best.<>
<>Hahaha.<>
<>You ever had station coffee?<>
<>No.<>
<>It's terrible. Come on, I'll make you a cup.<>
Adriana looks at you. You nod. She follows your $sis toward the mess hall.
They seem to to have connected well. Good to hear. $name_sis was too lonely after we escaped Haven. It's nice she got a friend.
<> <> <> <>

passages.name: p_station_task_mom
passages.source_raw:
<> <> You head to the crew quarter's common space. You find your $mom there. She's sitting on the edge of the sofa.


<>Hey.<>
<>Hey, sweetheart. Come in. Close the door.<>
You sit beside her. The couch barely fits both of you.
<>I read it. Twice. Once last night and once this morning.<>
<>And?<>
<>And... it's what I needed to hear. Even the parts that hurt. Especially those.<>
She picks up the envelope. Turns it over in her hands.
<>You know what's funny? I've been going back and forth with myself for months. Ever since we left Haven. One day I'd tell myself — let him go, focus on you and $name_sis, build something new. The next day I'd be staring at the cockpit door wondering if he was going to walk through it. Back and forth. Every single day. Like a pendulum that never settles.<>
<>And now?<>
<>Now it's settled. The letter settled it. He's not coming back. He can't come back. And he doesn't want me to spend the rest of my life waiting at a door that's never going to open.<>
She sets the envelope on the table. Gently, like it's fragile.
<>I needed closure, $name. That's the word for it. Closure. I didn't know I needed it until I had it.<>
<>He said he's happy there. I know that's hard to hear.<>
<>It is. And it isn't. I'd rather he be happy somewhere than suffering. Even if that somewhere isn't with me.<>
She looks at you. Her eyes are clear. Not wet, not red. She did her crying last night with the letter. This morning she's on the other side of it.
<>I spent so much time worrying about him that I forgot to worry about you. About $name_sis. About us. You've been flying across the galaxy, fighting the Federation, exploring new planets... And I feel I wasn't really there for you.<>
<>$mom—<>
<>No. Let me say this. I'm done waiting. I'm done looking backward. Whatever comes next, I'm here. With you.<>
She turns to you. Puts her hand on your face. Her palm is warm. She leans in and kisses you — on the lips. Soft, brief, but not the kind of kiss a $mom gives her $son. She holds it for a beat longer than she should. Then she pulls back.

Neither of you says anything about it..
<>Go get ready.<>
<> <> <> <>

passages.name: p_station_gabbie_goodbye
passages.source_raw:
<> <> You're in your room. Stuffing your bag — the drives, the data chip, a change of clothes, the few things you brought from the ship. The cot is stripped. The room looks like it did before you arrived. Like you were never here.

A knock.
<>Come in.<>
Gabbie. She's cleaned up — grease gone from her hands, hair down instead of pulled back under a bandana. Tank top, work pants, boots. She leans against the doorframe and looks at the empty room and the bag on the floor.
<>You're really going.<>
<>Yeah.<>
She steps inside. Closes the door behind her.
<>I didn't want to end things weird. With the docking bay conversation earlier — I was being— I don't know. I was being me. Which sometimes means being difficult.<>
<>You weren't being difficult.<>
<>I was a little difficult. It's fine. I own it.<>
She crosses the room. Stands in front of you. Close enough to touch.
<>No bad feelings, $name. I mean that. You've got your mission and your people and I've got my station and my life here. That's how it works. But before you go—<>
She puts her hand on the back of your neck and pulls you into a kiss. Soft, playful. The kind of kiss that says I'm not done with you but I know you're leaving so I'm going to make this one count.


<>I want this...<>
<> <> <>

passages.name: p_station_embark
passages.source_raw:
<> <> The docking bay. Your ship sits on the pad, panels sealed, hull clean — Gabbie's work. The sand is gone. The thruster housings gleam. She spent all morning on it and you both know why.

Your $mom walks up the ramp first. She runs her hand along the cabin wall as she enters — a small gesture, reacquainting herself with the ship she's lived in for months. She picks her seat without hesitating. Old habits.
Your $sis follows, bag over one shoulder, already pulling up something on her communicator. She drops into a seat and kicks her feet up on the one across from her.
<>Same ship. Same smell. Like old socks and recycled air. Missed it.<>
Adriana stands at the bottom of the ramp. Canvas bag in both hands. She looks up at the ship — the hull, the thrusters, the ramp.
<>You coming?<>
She walks up the ramp.
Gabbie is standing at the edge of the pad. Arms crossed, rag over her shoulder. She watches you from the bay floor. You look at her from the top of the ramp. She raises a hand and waves you goodbye. Then she drops it and turns toward the maintenance corridor.
<> <> <>

passages.name: p_station_liftoff
passages.source_raw:
<> <> You slide into the pilot seat. The controls are familiar — every switch, every gauge. Your hands settle into position from muscle memory.

Engine start. The cabin hums. The vibration climbs through the floor and into your seat. Behind you, Adriana grabs an armrest. Your $mom is strapping in. Your $sis is already strapped, eyes on her communicator.
<>Everyone hold on. Detaching in three.<>
The docking clamps release. A clunk, then a lurch, then the low push of thrusters guiding you out of the bay. The station drifts past the viewport — docking rings, solar panels, the blinking running lights. Getting smaller. Getting quieter.
Through the rear camera feed you see the docking bay doors closing. The station becomes a shape. Then a silhouette. Then a point of light among thousands of others.
<>It's gone.<>
<>Yeah.<>
You check the nav console. Pull up the long-range comms array. The rebel base frequency is saved from months ago — Jasper's encrypted channel. You punch it in.
<>Let's see if anyone's home.<>
<> <> <>

passages.name: p_station_jasper_call
passages.source_raw:
<> <> Static. Then a crackle. Then a voice you haven't heard in months — rough, clipped, the cadence of a man who's been giving orders so long his casual speech sounds like briefings.



<>...Identify. This is a restricted frequency.<>
<>Jasper, it's $name.<>
Silence. Two seconds. Three.
<>$name. Son of a— you're alive. We lost your signal weeks ago. Gemma wanted to send a search party. I told her to wait. I told her you'd make it back.<>
<>You were right.<>
<>Did you find him?<>
<>I found him. He's alive. He's on a planet called Paradiso — Federation black site, luxury prison. He can't leave. Biochip in his neck, tied to his vitals. Extraction isn't an option.<>
A pause. You can hear Jasper breathing. Processing.
<>Understood. And the mission? Did you find anything we can use?<>
<>Three encrypted drives from a former Project Echo researcher. Eighty-seven hours of lab footage, forty-three subject testimonies, and internal Federation memos proving they knew the implants were lethal and authorized continued testing. On top of that — a full data dump from a Federation monitoring bunker. Surveillance records, communication logs, the entire operational structure of the Gilded Cage program. And if we're lucky, my father's old access codes that might still open some doors.<>
Silence again. Longer this time.
<>Say that again.<>
<>You heard me, Jasper.<>
<>That's a weapon. If even half of that checks out, we can go public. Broadcast it across every system.<>
<>That's the idea. I'm heading to you now. What are the current base coordinates?<>
<>We moved. I'll send you the coords. Same approach vector as last time — drop out of hyperspace at the beacon and we'll guide you in. I'll have Gemma prep the landing bay.<>
A ping on the nav console. Coordinates received. You lock them in.
<>$name. One more thing.<>
<>Yeah?<>
<>Your father. Did he say anything about me?<>
<>He said to tell you that you were right about everything.<>
A long exhale on the other end of the line. The kind of breath you let out when something you carried for years finally gets set down.
<>That stubborn bastard. Took him long enough.<>
<>Get here safe, $name. We're waiting for you. Jasper out.<>
The comms click off. Static. Then silence.
You lean back in the pilot seat. The coordinates are locked. The nav computer calculates the jump — eighteen hours in hyperspace. You look over your shoulder. Your $mom is in the cabin, eyes closed. Your $sis is curled up in her seat. Adriana is staring out the side viewport at the stars like she'll never get tired of them.
<>Everyone hold on. Jumping in ten seconds.<>
You press the sequence. The engines build. The stars stretch. The cabin fills with blue-white light.


Hyperspace. The hum. The light. You grip the throttle and let the universe fold around you.
Next stop: the rebel base..
<> <> <>

passages.name: arrival_rebelbase
passages.source_raw:
<> <> The ship drops out of hyperspace and the rebel base fills the viewport. It's built into an asteroid — hollowed out, reinforced, a cluster of docking bays and antenna arrays bolted to the rock face like barnacles on a hull. Running lights blink in sequence along the approach corridor. Two fighter craft drift past on patrol, close enough to see the pilots through the canopies.

The comms crackle.
<>Unidentified vessel, this is Rebel Base Actual. Identify or get vaporized. We've had a long week.<>
<>Gemma, it's $name.<>
<>$name! Bay three is open. Bring her in slow.<>
You guide the ship through the approach corridor. The bay doors open — massive, industrial, nothing like the gas station's cramped dock. Inside, a proper hangar: fuel lines, maintenance rigs, three other ships in various states of repair. People moving with purpose. Uniforms, tool belts, cargo loaders. This is a military operation. Not a big one, but a real one.
The landing gear touches down. The engines wind. Silence.
Adriana is pressed against the viewport, eyes wide. Your $mom is standing behind you, one hand on the back of the pilot seat. Your $sis is already unbuckling.
<>About time. My legs are dead.<>
You lower the ramp. The hangar air hits you — recycled, metallic, oil and ozone. And standing at the bottom of the ramp, arms at his sides, looking older than you remember: Jasper.
He doesn't say anything for a second. Just looks at you. Then he steps forward and grabs you — not a handshake, a full embrace. One arm around your back, the other hand on the back of your head. He holds it for three seconds and lets go.
<>Not a scratch on you, kid.<>
<>Yeah, it went well, Jasper.<>
He looks past you. Your $mom is coming down the ramp..
<>$name_mom. It's been too long.<>
<>Hello Jasper..<>
<>Welcome. I'm glad you're all here.<>
Your $sis comes down. Jasper nods at her.
Adriana is last. She walks down the ramp slowly, canvas bag against her chest. Jasper looks at her, then at you, eyebrow raised.
<>This is Adriana. She's from Paradiso. She helped me get the intel. She's with us now.<>
<>From Paradiso itself?<>
<>Born there. Lived there twenty-five years.<>
Jasper looks at her for a long beat.
<>Welcome aboard. Any friend of $name's has a place here.<>
He claps his hands together.
<>Alright. I got you a residence — one of the family units in the housing block. Three rooms, kitchen, common area. It's not the Ritz but it's got walls, a roof, and the water's hot most of the time.<>
<>Three rooms? There's four of us.<>
<>I know. I didn't plan for—<>
<>It's fine. Adriana can stay with me. Right?<>
She looks at Adriana.
<>If you don't mind.<>
<>I don't snore. We'll be fine.<>
<>Good. That's settled. Let me show you the place, then $name and I have business at the command centre. I want to brief you on what we've been working on while you were gone.<>
<> <> <>

passages.name: arrival_rebelbase2
passages.source_raw:
<> <> Jasper leads you through the base. Corridors carved out of asteroid rock, reinforced with steel beams and insulated panels. People pass in both directions: mechanics, analysts, soldiers, a woman carrying a crate of medical supplies, a man arguing into a communicator. It's busy. It's alive. It's the opposite of Paradiso.

The housing block is a quieter section — a branching corridor with numbered doors. Jasper stops at unit 7. Presses his thumb to the lock. The door opens.
<>Home sweet home. Or as sweet as it gets when your home is inside a rock.<>
The residence is small but functional. Three doors off the main room, each leading to a bedroom. One small bathroom shared between all of them. There's a viewport in the common area showing the asteroid field outside — chunks of rock drifting in slow rotation against the stars.
Your $mom walks through the space. Opens a cabinet. Checks the water pressure at the sink. Runs her hand along the counter. She's already calculating how to make this work.
<>It's good. We've lived in worse.<>
After $name_mom , $name_sis and Adriana go to their rooms to check them out, Jasper approaches you. <>You did a good job keeping your family together through all of this, kid.<>
He puts his hand over your shoulder. <>Alright. Let the girls settle in. You and I have work to do. Command centre is this way.<>
<> <> <>

passages.name: arrival_rebelbase3
passages.source_raw:
<> <> The command centre is the heart of the base. A large circular room carved from the asteroid core, walls lined with screens, a holo-table in the centre projecting a slowly rotating star map. Workstations around the perimeter, each manned by a rebel analyst or comms officer. The room hums with chatter, keyboard clicks, and the low pulse of the holo-projector.

Gemma is leaning over the holo-table when you walk in. She looks up.
<>$name. In one piece. Mostly.<>
<>Gemma. Good to see you.<>
<>Good to see you too.<>
Jasper activates the holo-table. The star map zooms in on a system you don't recognize — a single yellow sun, four planets, the third one highlighted in green.
<>This is the Varen system. Outer rim, barely on Federation maps. The third planet is called Erden. Agricultural world — farms, grain fields, livestock, orchards. Population of about forty thousand spread across a dozen settlements. No military presence worth mentioning. The Federation runs it with a skeleton crew: one garrison of thirty soldiers, a regional governor, and a supply chain that ships ninety percent of the planet's food output directly to Federation core worlds.<>
<>Forty thousand people growing food they never get to eat. The Federation takes everything and ships in processed rations as payment. The locals have been angry for years. Last month, three settlements refused the harvest shipment. The Federation sent the garrison to force compliance. They beat a farmer in front of his family. That was the tipping point.<>
<>We've been in contact with the local resistance for six weeks. They've got numbers but no weapons. Pitchforks and hunting rifles against Federation armour. They need help.<>
<>And that's where we come in.<>
<>That's where you come in. If we can arm the locals and help them push the garrison out, we don't just win a battle. We win a planet. An agricultural planet. Food production, $name. The one thing every rebel cell, every refugee camp, every free settlement in the outer rim is desperate for.<>
<>What's the Federation's response going to look like?<>
<>That's the beauty of it. Erden is low priority — outer rim, no strategic value beyond agriculture. The Federation won't deploy a fleet over a farming dispute. They'll send reinforcements from the nearest garrison, which is three systems away. That gives us a window. If the uprising succeeds before those reinforcements arrive, the Federation has to decide whether retaking a grain planet is worth the resources.<>
<>And the Paradiso data? The drives?<>
<>That's phase two. Once we have Erden, we have a platform. A legitimate base with a population and infrastructure. We broadcast the Project Echo footage from there — not as rebels hiding in an asteroid, but as a free planet making an accusation.<>
<>One thing at a time, though. First Erden. Then the broadcast. The whole galaxy will see the Federation crimes and they will also have Erden as the perfect example that you can rebel and win. We are hoping that sparks something on the people.<>
<> <> <>

passages.name: arrival_rebelbase4
passages.source_raw:
<> <><><><> Gemma pulls up a series of images on the holo-table. Satellite photos of Erden's surface — green fields stretching to the horizon, dotted with farmsteads and silos. A small town with a central square and a clock tower.

<>This is Millhaven, the largest settlement. Population eight thousand. The Federation garrison is here — this compound on the north side of town.<>
She zooms in. A walled compound with prefab barracks, a comms tower, two armoured transports parked inside the perimeter. Thirty soldiers. It's not a fortress. It's a police station with a fence.
<>Thirty Federation troops. Light armour, standard rifles, two transport vehicles. No air support. No orbital presence. Their comms relay connects to the nearest Federation outpost in the Kessler system — three days away at military speed. That's our window.<>
<>What do you need from me?<>
<>You fly to Erden. Alone — one ship draws less attention than a convoy. You land outside Millhaven, make contact with their leader, and deliver the weapons. We've got a cargo of rifles, sidearms, ammunition, and comm equipment ready to load onto your ship. Enough to arm two hundred fighters.<>
She pulls up a map of the region around Millhaven — fields, tree lines, a river cutting through the valley. A red circle marks a location south of town.
<>This is the drop zone. An abandoned grain silo three kilometres south of town, in the tree line. You hand off the weapons, help them coordinate the assault on the garrison, and get out.<>
<>This isn't a combat mission, $name. Not primarily. You're a smuggler and a coordinator. You get the weapons in, you help them plan, and you let the locals fight their own war.<>
<>And if it goes wrong?<>
<>Then you get on your ship and you leave. You're no good to anyone dead. The drives, the data, your father's codes — that's bigger than one planet. If Erden falls, we regroup and try somewhere else. But I don't think it will fall. These people have been waiting for a reason to fight. We're giving them one.<>
<>I'll load the cargo tonight. Your ship will be prepped and ready by morning. Take the night to rest, see your family, get your head right.<>
<>Any questions?<>
<>When do I leave?<>
<>Soon. For now — go home, $name. Eat something. Sleep in a proper bed. You've earned a night off.<>
He puts his hand on your shoulder. Squeezes once.
<>I'm glad you're here. We all are.<>
<> <> <> <> <> <>

passages.name: rb_terminal
passages.source_raw:
<> <> <> You sit at the desk and boot the terminal. The rebel network is basic but functional — internal comms, mission briefs, a shared intel database, and a surprisingly large media archive someone uploaded for morale.


<> <>You read through the latest intel reports on Federation troop movements. Three patrol routes near the outer rim have shifted — could mean reinforcements to Erden, could mean nothing. <>You review the Erden mission parameters for the fourth time. Drop zone coordinates, garrison layout, local contact protocols. You could recite them in your sleep. <>You find a message board where rebels post updates from across the frontier. A settlement on Karis V successfully resisted a Federation tax raid. A refugee convoy made it to the neutral zone. Small victories, scattered across the galaxy. <>You browse the media archive. Someone uploaded three hundred old Earth films. You watch ten minutes of something in black and white about a man in a desert before the terminal crashes and reboots. <>You check the encrypted comms channel. Nothing new from Jasper. Nothing from the Erden contacts. Silence can mean peace or it can mean something else. You close the terminal. <>
<>

<> <>You think about Paradiso. You remember your time there and wonder how they are doing. <>You think about your father on the terrace, glass in hand, watching a sunset he's seen a thousand times. <>You think about Erden. Farmers with pitchforks against Federation armour. You're about to give them a fighting chance. <>You don't think about anything. Just the hum. Just the dark behind your eyes. It's enough. <>

passages.name: rb_sleep
passages.source_raw:
<> <> <> <> <> <> <>
<> <> You dream about soft skin and warm breath against your neck. Someone's thigh draped over yours. You can't see her face but she smells like jasmine.
<> A dream. Hands on your chest, sliding down. A mouth at your ear whispering something you can't quite hear. Your hips move on their own.
<> You dream about a woman riding you in a room you don't recognize. She's moving slow, her hair falling across her face. You reach for her and she pushes your hands down.
<> Hot water. A shower. Someone behind you, arms around your waist, lips on your shoulder blade. Steam everywhere. You can't tell who it is and you don't care.
<> A dream about a mouth. Slow. Wet. Looking up at you through hair you almost recognize. You wake up hard and breathing fast.
<> You dream about the lagoon. Bioluminescent water. A woman swimming toward you, naked, her body glowing blue. She wraps her legs around you in the warm current.
<> A bed you've never been in. Silk sheets. A woman on all fours, looking over her shoulder at you. She says your name and it sounds like a dare.
<> You dream about hands pulling you down. A couch. A woman underneath you, legs wrapped tight, her back arching off the cushions. The sound she makes stays with you after you wake up.
<> Someone straddling you in the dark. You can feel everything — the weight, the warmth, the rhythm. She leans down and bites your lip. You wake up tangled in the sheets.
<> A dream about a woman pressed against a wall. Your hands on her hips. She wraps one leg around you and pulls you closer. The wall is cold and she's not.
<> You dream about flying. The cockpit, the stars, the hum of the engine. No destination. Just black and light and the feeling of going somewhere that doesn't exist yet. <> You dream about Haven. The parks. Rain on the grass. A house you lived in once that probably doesn't exist anymore. You're standing in the doorway and you can't decide whether to go in or walk away. <> No dreams. Just warm dark and the hum of the station. The best sleep you've had in weeks. <> You dream about Erden. Green fields, dirt roads, a clock tower. Farmers with rifles. A woman you haven't met yet standing in a field of grain, waiting for something. <> You dream about your father on the terrace. Sunset. He's holding a glass and watching the sky. He doesn't turn around. You try to say something but the words don't come. The sun goes down and he's still there. <>
<> <> <>

passages.name: rb_command_gemma
passages.source_raw:
<> <> <> You pull a chair up to Gemma's workstation. The screen is dense — intercepted transmissions, patrol routes, supply manifests. She talks without looking away from it.

<>These are garrison comm logs from the last three weeks. I need someone to cross-reference patrol times against the shift rotations we pulled from that stolen datapad.<>
You spend the next hour sifting through timestamps and callsigns. Most of it is routine. Some of it isn't. You tap the screen where two entries don't line up.

<>Hold on. Look at these three nights — the fourteenth, seventeenth, twentieth. Same callsign on the east wall, same forty-minute dead zone between sweeps. That's not a rotation overlap. That's a hole.<>
Gemma leans in. Her eyes move across the timestamps. She pulls the patrol map onto the holo-table and overlays the shift data.

<>There. See that gap? Forty minutes between patrol sweeps on the east wall, every third night. That's not random — that's understaffing. They don't have the bodies to cover it.<>
She marks it on the holo-table. A thin red line blinks along the eastern perimeter of the garrison compound.

<>Good catch, $name.<>

<>
@@color:deepskyblue;INT +2@@
<> <> <>

passages.name: rb_command_jasper
passages.source_raw:
<> <> <> You step up to the holo-table. Erden's garrison compound floats in blue wireframe — walls, guard towers, the main gate, the motor pool off to the south. Jasper has drawn approach vectors in yellow, three of them, converging from different angles.

<>Two problems. First — the ridge here gives us cover on approach, but it funnels us into a killzone if they spot us early. Second — we don't know if those AA batteries are automated or crewed.<>
He zooms in on the south wall. Two turret emplacements blink red.

<>If they're automated, we can jam them. If they're crewed, we need a diversion team drawing fire while the main force breaches. Two completely different plans depending on one piece of intel we don't have yet.<>
You study the approach vectors. Something's missing from the overlay. You drag the map south and tap the terrain layer.

<>What about this? There's a drainage channel running along the south side. Old municipal infrastructure — it's not on your overlay but it's on the geological survey. If it's still open, that's a covered approach straight to the south wall. No ridge, no killzone, no guessing about the AA.<>
<>...Huh. You're right. That's old municipal infrastructure. Might still be open. Might be a third option nobody's mapped.<>
He marks it in green and leans back, rubbing his jaw.

<>Not bad. I'll send a recon drone tonight to check if it's passable. Thanks, $name.<>
<>
@@color:deepskyblue;INT +2@@
<> <> <>

passages.name: rb_command_briefing
passages.source_raw:
<> <> <> The holo-table is fully active — the garrison compound in sharp blue wireframe, troop markers pulsing in red, supply lines threaded in yellow. Gemma stands on one side with a datapad. Jasper on the other, arms folded, studying the projection like it owes him money.

<>Alright. Here's where we are. Three approach vectors. North ridge gives us elevation but no cover past the treeline. East wall has that patrol gap Gemma found — forty-minute window every third night. South drainage channel is unconfirmed but promising.<>
He taps the table. The three vectors light up in green, staggered.

<>The gap is reliable. I've confirmed it across three weeks of intercepted logs. They rotate a twelve-man detail on a section built for twenty. That's not a gap — that's a hemorrhage.<>
<>Which means either they're stretched thin or they want us to think they are.<>
<>They're stretched thin, Jasper. Their requisition traffic is begging for reinforcements every other day. Nobody fakes that kind of paperwork desperation.<>
Jasper grunts. Zooms into the motor pool on the south end. Four armored transports parked in a row, fuel depot adjacent.

<>If we hit the fuel depot first, those transports are scrap. No pursuit, no rapid response to the outer settlements. But that means splitting the assault team before we've even breached the walls.<>
<>Not if the diversion team handles it. Small unit, demo charges, in and out before the main force hits the east wall. Timing has to be tight though. Two minutes off and the whole thing unravels.<>
They both look at you. Jasper tilts his head toward the holo-table.

<>You've been staring at this thing long enough. What do you see that we're missing?<>
You step closer to the projection. Rotate the compound north. The comm tower sits on the far side — a single dish array, lightly guarded, feeding every radio in the garrison.

<>The comm tower. You're both thinking about what to hit inside the walls, but if we take the tower out first — before the fuel depot, before the breach — they can't call for reinforcement. No distress signal, no off-base QRF scrambling to flank us. The diversion team doesn't need to blow the motor pool if the garrison is already deaf and mute. We buy more time on every phase.<>
Gemma pulls up the comm tower specs on her datapad. Studies it for a few seconds.

<>Single hardline relay, one dish array. Two charges would do it. Three to be safe.<>
<>That reshuffles the whole order of operations. Comm tower, then east wall breach, then motor pool cleanup after we've already got boots inside.<>
He looks at Gemma. She nods once — short, definitive.

<>Good. That's cleaner. I like it better. $name, you just saved us a headache and probably a few lives.<>
<>
@@color:deepskyblue;INT +2@@
<> <> <>

passages.name: rb_command_talk
passages.source_raw:
<> <> <> <> You pull up a chair next to Jasper. The coffee is terrible but he pours you one anyway. You talk about various subjects — old missions, people you've lost, places you'd go if the war ended tomorrow. He doesn't say much that's new but he says it like he means it. That counts for something out here.

<>
@@color:#f23f3f;CHA +3@@
<> <> <> You grab a chair and drag it over. The metal legs screech against the floor. Jasper doesn't flinch — just slides a dented mug across the table and fills it from a thermos that's seen better decades.

The holo-table hums between you, Erden rotating in dim blue. For a while neither of you says anything. The silence isn't awkward. It's the kind that only works between people who've been shot at together.

<>Can I ask you something? And I don't want the answer you think I want to hear.<>
<>Go ahead.<>
<>What happens after? Say we pull this off. Say we crack that garrison wide open, expose the Federation for what they are. The broadcasts go out, the colonies see the truth. Then what?<>
He stares into his coffee. Swirls it once.

<>Because I've been thinking about it more than I should. The fighting part — that I understand. Point me at the problem, give me a squad, I'll figure it out. I've been doing that since I was nineteen. But the part that comes after...<>
He trails off. The holo-table flickers — a brief glitch in Erden's southern hemisphere, then it stabilizes.

<>Someone has to rebuild all of it. Infrastructure. Government. Courts. Schools. Everything the Federation hollowed out over thirty years. And everyone's going to look around the room for the person who should lead that, and I...<>
He exhales through his nose. Sets the mug down.

<>I'm not that guy, $name. I know how to break things. I know how to keep people alive in a firefight. But rebuilding? Governance? Standing in front of a crowd and telling them it's going to be okay when half the supply chains are wrecked and everyone's hungry and angry and looking for someone to blame?<>
<>You're selling yourself short. You already lead people. You already make the calls nobody else wants to make. That doesn't stop being useful just because the guns go quiet.<>
<>Leading a rebel base and leading a whole damn empire aren't the same thing. I'd be faking it. And people can smell that. They'd follow me into a fight because I've earned that. But peacetime leadership is a different animal entirely. I'd burn out or screw it up or both.<>
<>Then don't do it alone. Nobody's asking you to be a one-man government. You just said it yourself — you know how to keep people alive. That's not nothing. Find the ones who know how to build and let them build. You watch the door.<>
He picks the mug back up. Drinks. Winces at the taste.

<>I just hope someone steps up. Someone who actually wants to build something and not just sit in the chair the Federation left warm. Because if nobody does, we'll win this war and lose everything that comes after.<>
The holo-table keeps turning. Erden's blue glow catches the lines around his eyes. He looks older in this light. Tired in a way sleep doesn't fix.

<>Anyway. That's what keeps me up at night. Not the garrison. Not the assault. The morning after, when the smoke clears and everyone turns around and says "now what."<>
He tops off your mug without asking. You sit with him a while longer. The coffee never gets better but the company does.

<>
@@color:#f23f3f;CHA +3@@
<> <> <> <>

passages.name: rb_mq_erden_briefing
passages.source_raw:
<> <> The command centre is louder than usual. Two analysts arguing over a printout. A comms officer with her headset half off, pinching the bridge of her nose. The holo-table already lit and rotating Erden over the room.

Jasper spots you and waves you in without breaking off from Gemma.

<>Sit down, $name.<>
You sit. Erden turns slowly above the table — green, brown, two small ice caps. It looks peaceful from up here.

<>Here's the thing. We're not sending you in with the cargo. Not yet. Everything we have on that system came from a farmer with a smuggled comm six weeks ago and I'm not putting a ship full of rifles into the dark on that.<>
<>So you're going to take a look first. In and out. No landing, no contact. If anyone asks afterwards, you weren't there.<>
<>What am I looking at?<>
Gemma taps the table. The view drops to a schematic — yellow sun, four planets, a thin asteroid belt.

<>Mostly we want to know if their orbital array is still on. It's an old low-orbit grid, Federation installed it maybe ten years ago..<>
<>Other thing we want pictures. Millhaven, the garrison compound, anything on the surface that wasn't on the survey maps the last time anyone bothered to update them. If there's a new installation somewhere we need to know before we put a ship down in those fields.<>
<>And if the array pings me?<>
<>You turn around and you come home. We try something else. Don't get clever about it.<>
<>We pulled the heavy plating off your ship and dropped a passive scanner suite in. She's lighter, she's quieter, and she will absolutely lose a fight, so don't pick one. The whole run should take you nine or ten hours if nothing goes wrong.<>
<>She's in bay two. Gemma'll walk you through the new console before you launch.<>
<>When do you want me out?<>
<>Today if you can stomach it. Tomorrow if you can't.<>
You look at the planet for a second longer.

<> <> <> <>

passages.name: rb_ship_gemma
passages.source_raw:
<> <> The hangar smells of ozone, burnt flux, and cold hydraulic fluid. The ambient hum of the asteroid's life support is drowned out by the sporadic whine of a plasma torch.

Gemma is half-submerged under the open access panel of a sleek, battered light freighter. She’s wearing grease-stained overalls, the top half peeled down and tied around her waist, leaving her in a sweat-dampened grey tank top.



<>What's the damage?<>
She slides out on a mechanic's creeper, wiping a streak of black grease across her forehead with the back of her wrist. She looks tired, but her eyes are sharp.

<>Coolant manifold is shot. The Federation patrol over Oakhaven winged one of our scout ships. I'm trying to patch the bypass before the pilot realizes I'm cannibalizing parts from the ventilation system.<>
<>Sounds safe.<>
<>Safe is a luxury we left behind in the core worlds. Grab that hydro-spanner. The red one. I need you to hold the coupling steady while I weld the seal.<>
You grab the heavy tool and slide in beside her under the ship's hull. The space is incredibly cramped. Your shoulder presses flush against hers. You can feel the heat radiating off her skin, smell the sharp tang of sweat and machine oil.

<>Right there. Don't move.<>
She leans over you to reach the panel, her chest brushing lightly against your arm. Her focus is absolute, the blue light of the plasma torch illuminating her face. You watch the steady pulse of the vein in her neck.

<>Got it.<>
She powers down the torch. In the sudden quiet of the cramped space, she doesn't immediately pull away. Her face is only inches from yours. She looks at your eyes, then down to your mouth for a fraction of a second, before clearing her throat and sliding back out.

<>Good hands, $name. Thanks. I'll get the rest of this. Go get some rest. You've got Erden to think about.<>
You catch a slight flush on her neck that wasn't there a minute ago.

<> <> <> <> <>

passages.name: rb_ship_cockpit
passages.source_raw:
<> <> <> <> You climb the ramp and slide into the pilot seat. The console lights up — fuel levels, thruster status, nav alignment, sensor array. Everything reads green.

You pull up the sensor calibration module. The array drifted slightly, nothing critical, but a few degrees off on the long-range scanners could mean the difference between spotting a Federation patrol at ten thousand clicks or five hundred.

You run the diagnostic, adjust the gain on the forward array, sync the lateral sensors to the updated star chart, and lock it in. The console beeps twice. Green across the board.
<>
@@color:deepskyblue;INT +2@@
<> <> <>

passages.name: rb_mq_erden_launch
passages.source_raw:
<><> <> Bay two is quieter than the main hangar. Your ship is up on her struts, ramp down, two techs finishing up under the starboard nacelle. Gemma's already at the foot of the ramp with a tablet under her arm.

<>Come up. I want you sitting in it before I explain anything.<>
You follow her up the ramp into the cockpit. The seat smells like fresh polymer. The whole forward bank has been gutted and replaced — half the panels are still showing their bare housings.


<>Your old console is in a crate somewhere. This is an state-of-the-art one, premium scanners, interceptors...<>
She leans over and taps the centre display. A grid blooms across the screen — soft blue, slow refresh.

<>Left side is the spatial feed. Anything pinging an active sensor anywhere near you shows up here. If this lights up, it means something is looking. Doesn't mean it found you, just means it's looking. You see it light up, you assume the worst.<>
<>And the right side?<>
<>Optical. Cameras under the belly, one in the nose. That's how you bring back pictures. The shutter is this — here. You hold it down for continuous, tap for single frame. Everything caches to a black box I can pull when you get back.<>
She straightens up and crosses her arms.

<>Don't touch anything you don't recognise. If it starts beeping at you, that's the proximity alarm and you should already be turning around.<>
<>Got it.<>
<>Come back in one piece, $name. I had to fight Jasper for the budget on this thing.<>
She knocks her knuckles twice against the doorframe and heads back down the ramp.

<> <> <>

passages.name: rb_gym_bag
passages.source_raw:
<> <> <> <> <>You work the heavy bag for twenty minutes. Jab, cross, hook. The chain rattles with every hit. Your knuckles sting through the wraps. The bag doesn't complain.

<>Combinations. Three-piece, four-piece, body-head-body. The bag swings wide on a hook and you reset. Again. Again. The rhythm takes over and your brain goes quiet.

<>You hit the bag until your arms are dead. Then you hit it some more. A rebel walks by, watches for a second, and moves on. You don't notice.

<>Low kicks, body shots, uppercuts. The bag is held together with tape and stubbornness. Kind of like everything else on this base.

<>
<>

passages.name: rb_gym_weights
passages.source_raw:
<> <> <> <> <>Bench press. Three sets of twelve. Your chest burns.
